Let  
\[
\mathbf y_i=(y_{i1},\dots,y_{in_i})^\top,\qquad 
\mathbf x_i=(x_{i1},\dots,x_{in_i})^\top,\qquad 
Z_i=\begin{pmatrix}1&x_{i1}\\ \vdots&\vdots\\ 1&x_{in_i}\end{pmatrix},
\]
and \(\theta=(\beta_0,\beta)^\top\). Conditional on \(u_i\),
\[
\mathbf y_i\mid u_i \sim N(Z_i\theta+u_i\mathbf 1_i,\ \sigma_e^2 I_{n_i}),
\qquad 
u_i\sim N(0,\sigma_u^2).
\]

---

## (1) Complete-data log-likelihood

The complete data are \((\mathbf y_i,u_i)\), \(i=1,\dots,k\). Conditioning on the covariates \(x_{ij}\), the complete-data likelihood is

\[
L_c(\theta)
=
\prod_{i=1}^k
\left[
\frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi\sigma_u^2}}
\exp\left\{-\frac{u_i^2}{2\sigma_u^2}\right\}
\prod_{j=1}^{n_i}
\frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi\sigma_e^2}}
\exp\left\{
-\frac{(y_{ij}-\beta_0-\beta x_{ij}-u_i)^2}{2\sigma_e^2}
\right\}
\right].
\]

Therefore the complete-data log-likelihood is

\[
\ell_c(\theta)
=
-\frac12\sum_{i=1}^k
\left[
\log(2\pi\sigma_u^2)+\frac{u_i^2}{\sigma_u^2}
+n_i\log(2\pi\sigma_e^2)
+\frac{1}{\sigma_e^2}
\sum_{j=1}^{n_i}
(y_{ij}-\beta_0-\beta x_{ij}-u_i)^2
\right].
\]

Equivalently, up to constants not depending on \(\theta\),

\[
\ell_c(\theta)
=
-\frac{1}{2\sigma_e^2}
\sum_{i=1}^k\sum_{j=1}^{n_i}
(y_{ij}-\beta_0-\beta x_{ij}-u_i)^2
-\frac{1}{2\sigma_u^2}\sum_{i=1}^k u_i^2.
\]

---

## (2) EM algorithm with \(\sigma_u^2,\sigma_e^2\) known

At iteration \(t\), suppose the current parameter value is

\[
\theta^{(t)}=(\beta_0^{(t)},\beta^{(t)})^\top.
\]

Define the current residuals

\[
r_{ij}^{(t)}=y_{ij}-\beta_0^{(t)}-\beta^{(t)}x_{ij},
\qquad 
r_i^{(t)}=\mathbf y_i-Z_i\theta^{(t)}.
\]

### E-step

We need the conditional distribution of \(u_i\mid \mathbf y_i,\theta^{(t)}\).

By normal conjugacy,

\[
u_i\mid \mathbf y_i,\theta^{(t)}
\sim
N\left(m_i^{(t)},\,v_i\right),
\]

where

\[
v_i
=
\left(\frac1{\sigma_u^2}+\frac{n_i}{\sigma_e^2}\right)^{-1}
=
\frac{\sigma_u^2\sigma_e^2}{\sigma_e^2+n_i\sigma_u^2},
\]

and

\[
m_i^{(t)}
=
E(u_i\mid \mathbf y_i,\theta^{(t)})
=
v_i\frac{1}{\sigma_e^2}
\sum_{j=1}^{n_i}
\left(y_{ij}-\beta_0^{(t)}-\beta^{(t)}x_{ij}\right).
\]

Equivalently,

\[
m_i^{(t)}
=
\frac{\sigma_u^2}{\sigma_e^2+n_i\sigma_u^2}
\sum_{j=1}^{n_i}
r_{ij}^{(t)}.
\]

Also,

\[
E(u_i^2\mid \mathbf y_i,\theta^{(t)})
=
v_i+\left(m_i^{(t)}\right)^2.
\]

Thus the EM auxiliary function is

\[
Q(\theta\mid \theta^{(t)})
=
E\{\ell_c(\theta)\mid \mathbf y,\theta^{(t)}\}.
\]

Dropping terms not depending on \(\theta\), this is

\[
Q(\theta\mid \theta^{(t)})
=
-\frac{1}{2\sigma_e^2}
\sum_{i=1}^k\sum_{j=1}^{n_i}
\left[
\left(y_{ij}-\beta_0-\beta x_{ij}-m_i^{(t)}\right)^2+v_i
\right]
+\text{terms not depending on }\theta.
\]

Since \(v_i\) does not depend on \(\theta\), the M-step reduces to least squares.

---

### M-step

Maximize \(Q(\theta\mid\theta^{(t)})\), equivalently minimize

\[
\sum_{i=1}^k\sum_{j=1}^{n_i}
\left(y_{ij}-m_i^{(t)}-\beta_0-\beta x_{ij}\right)^2.
\]

Thus we regress the adjusted responses

\[
y_{ij}^{*,(t)}=y_{ij}-m_i^{(t)}
\]

on an intercept and \(x_{ij}\).

Let

\[
z_{ij}=
\begin{pmatrix}
1\\
x_{ij}
\end{pmatrix}.
\]

Then

\[
\theta^{(t+1)}
=
\left(\sum_{i=1}^k\sum_{j=1}^{n_i} z_{ij}z_{ij}^\top\right)^{-1}
\left(\sum_{i=1}^k\sum_{j=1}^{n_i} z_{ij}\left(y_{ij}-m_i^{(t)}\right)\right).
\]

Equivalently, define

\[
N=\sum_i n_i,\qquad 
S_x=\sum_{i,j}x_{ij},\qquad 
S_{xx}=\sum_{i,j}x_{ij}^2,
\]

and

\[
T_0^{(t)}=\sum_{i,j}\left(y_{ij}-m_i^{(t)}\right),
\qquad 
T_1^{(t)}=\sum_{i,j}x_{ij}\left(y_{ij}-m_i^{(t)}\right).
\]

Then

\[
D=NS_{xx}-S_x^2,
\]

and

\[
\beta_0^{(t+1)}
=
\frac{S_{xx}T_0^{(t)}-S_xT_1^{(t)}}{D},
\]

\[
\beta^{(t+1)}
=
\frac{NT_1^{(t)}-S_xT_0^{(t)}}{D}.
\]

Iterate the E-step and M-step until convergence.

At convergence, the EM estimate equals the GLS/MLE estimator from the marginal model

\[
\mathbf y_i\sim N(Z_i\theta,\ V_i),
\qquad 
V_i=\sigma_e^2I_{n_i}+\sigma_u^2\mathbf 1_i\mathbf 1_i^\top.
\]

Thus

\[
\widehat\theta_{\text{MLE}}
=
\left(\sum_i Z_i^\top V_i^{-1}Z_i\right)^{-1}
\left(\sum_i Z_i^\top V_i^{-1}\mathbf y_i\right).
\]

---

## (3) Simulation and Monte Carlo MSE

Here is self-contained R code implementing the EM algorithm directly, without calling `lme4`, `nlme`, etc.

```r
## Parameters
k <- 30
n <- 20
N <- k * n

sigma_u2 <- 1
sigma_e2 <- 1.5

theta.true <- c(beta0 = 0.5, beta = 1.5)

## Generate one dataset
gen.data <- function() {
  id <- rep(seq_len(k), each = n)
  x <- runif(N, min = 10, max = 60)
  u <- rnorm(k, mean = 0, sd = sqrt(sigma_u2))
  eps <- rnorm(N, mean = 0, sd = sqrt(sigma_e2))
  y <- theta.true["beta0"] + theta.true["beta"] * x + u[id] + eps
  list(y = y, x = x, id = id)
}

## EM algorithm
em.lmm <- function(y, x, id, sigma_u2, sigma_e2,
                   tol = 1e-10, maxit = 10000) {
  
  X <- cbind(1, x)
  colnames(X) <- c("Intercept", "x")
  
  ## Use ordinary least squares as starting value, computed directly
  theta <- as.numeric(solve(crossprod(X), crossprod(X, y)))
  
  fac <- factor(id)
  g <- as.integer(fac)
  G <- nlevels(fac)
  ni <- as.numeric(tabulate(g, nbins = G))
  
  ## Posterior variances of u_i; do not depend on theta
  post.var <- 1 / (1 / sigma_u2 + ni / sigma_e2)
  
  XtX <- crossprod(X)
  
  for (iter in seq_len(maxit)) {
    
    ## E-step
    resid <- y - as.numeric(X %*% theta)
    sum.resid <- as.numeric(rowsum(resid, group = g, reorder = TRUE))
    
    m <- post.var * sum.resid / sigma_e2
    
    ## M-step
    y.star <- y - m[g]
    theta.new <- as.numeric(solve(XtX, crossprod(X, y.star)))
    
    if (max(abs(theta.new - theta)) < tol * (1 + max(abs(theta)))) {
      theta <- theta.new
      break
    }
    
    theta <- theta.new
  }
  
  names(theta) <- c("beta0", "beta")
  list(theta = theta, iter = iter)
}

## One simulated dataset
set.seed(2022)
dat1 <- gen.data()
fit1 <- em.lmm(dat1$y, dat1$x, dat1$id, sigma_u2, sigma_e2)

fit1$theta
fit1$iter
```

To repeat the experiment 100 times and compute Monte Carlo MSE:

```r
set.seed(2023)

B <- 100
est <- matrix(NA_real_, nrow = B, ncol = 2)
colnames(est) <- c("beta0", "beta")

for (b in seq_len(B)) {
  dat <- gen.data()
  fit <- em.lmm(dat$y, dat$x, dat$id, sigma_u2, sigma_e2)
  est[b, ] <- fit$theta
}

err <- sweep(est, 2, theta.true, "-")

mse <- colMeans(err^2)
mse

total.mse <- sum(mse)
total.mse
```

The Monte Carlo MSEs being estimated are

\[
\widehat{\operatorname{MSE}}(\widehat\beta_0)
=
\frac1{100}\sum_{b=1}^{100}
\left(\widehat\beta_{0,b}-0.5\right)^2,
\]

and

\[
\widehat{\operatorname{MSE}}(\widehat\beta)
=
\frac1{100}\sum_{b=1}^{100}
\left(\widehat\beta_b-1.5\right)^2.
\]

Because the simulation is random, the exact numbers depend on the seed. For this design, one should expect approximately

\[
\operatorname{MSE}(\widehat\beta_0)\approx 5.1\times 10^{-2},
\qquad
\operatorname{MSE}(\widehat\beta)\approx 1.3\times 10^{-5}.
\]

The slope MSE is much smaller because the covariate \(x_{ij}\) has a large spread over \([10,60]\), while the intercept corresponds to extrapolating to \(x=0\), which is outside the observed covariate range.

\[
N=\sum_i n_i,\qquad 
S_x=\sum_{i,j}x_{ij},\qquad 
S_{xx}=\sum_{i,j}x_{ij}^2,
\]

and

\[
T_0^{(t)}=\sum_{i,j}\left(y_{ij}-m_i^{(t)}\right),
\qquad 
T_1^{(t)}=\sum_{i,j}x_{ij}\left(y_{ij}-m_i^{(t)}\right).
\]

Then

\[
D=NS_{xx}-S_x^2,
\]

and

\[
\beta_0^{(t+1)}
=
\frac{S_{xx}T_0^{(t)}-S_xT_1^{(t)}}{D},
\]

\[
\beta^{(t+1)}
=
\frac{NT_1^{(t)}-S_xT_0^{(t)}}{D}.
\]

Iterate the E-step and M-step until convergence.

At convergence, the EM estimate equals the GLS/MLE estimator from the marginal model

\[
\mathbf y_i\sim N(Z_i\theta,\ V_i),
\qquad 
V_i=\sigma_e^2I_{n_i}+\sigma_u^2\mathbf 1_i\mathbf 1_i^\top.
\]

Thus

\[
\widehat\theta_{\text{MLE}}
=
\left(\sum_i Z_i^\top V_i^{-1}Z_i\right)^{-1}
\left(\sum_i Z_i^\top V_i^{-1}\mathbf y_i\right).
\]

---

## (3) Simulation and Monte Carlo MSE

Here is self-contained R code implementing the EM algorithm directly, without calling `lme4`, `nlme`, etc.

```r
## Parameters
k <- 30
n <- 20
N <- k * n

sigma_u2 <- 1
sigma_e2 <- 1.5

theta.true <- c(beta0 = 0.5, beta = 1.5)

## Generate one dataset
gen.data <- function() {
  id <- rep(seq_len(k), each = n)
  x <- runif(N, min = 10, max = 60)
  u <- rnorm(k, mean = 0, sd = sqrt(sigma_u2))
  eps <- rnorm(N, mean = 0, sd = sqrt(sigma_e2))
  y <- theta.true["beta0"] + theta.true["beta"] * x + u[id] + eps
  list(y = y, x = x, id = id)
}

## EM algorithm
em.lmm <- function(y, x, id, sigma_u2, sigma_e2,
                   tol = 1e-10, maxit = 10000) {
  
  X <- cbind(1, x)
  colnames(X) <- c("Intercept", "x")
  
  ## Use ordinary least squares as starting value, computed directly
  theta <- as.numeric(solve(crossprod(X), crossprod(X, y)))
  
  fac <- factor(id)
  g <- as.integer(fac)
  G <- nlevels(fac)
  ni <- as.numeric(tabulate(g, nbins = G))
  
  ## Posterior variances of u_i; do not depend on theta
  post.var <- 1 / (1 / sigma_u2 + ni / sigma_e2)
  
  XtX <- crossprod(X)
  
  for (iter in seq_len(maxit)) {
    
    ## E-step
    resid <- y - as.numeric(X %*% theta)
    sum.resid <- as.numeric(rowsum(resid, group = g, reorder = TRUE))
    
    m <- post.var * sum.resid / sigma_e2
    
    ## M-step
    y.star <- y - m[g]
    theta.new <- as.numeric(solve(XtX, crossprod(X, y.star)))
    
    if (max(abs(theta.new - theta)) < tol * (1 + max(abs(theta)))) {
      theta <- theta.new
      break
    }
    
    theta <- theta.new
  }
  
  names(theta) <- c("beta0", "beta")
  list(theta = theta, iter = iter)
}

## One simulated dataset
set.seed(2022)
dat1 <- gen.data()
fit1 <- em.lmm(dat1$y, dat1$x, dat1$id, sigma_u2, sigma_e2)

fit1$theta
fit1$iter
```

To repeat the experiment 100 times and compute Monte Carlo MSE:

```r
set.seed(2023)

B <- 100
est <- matrix(NA_real_, nrow = B, ncol = 2)
colnames(est) <- c("beta0", "beta")

for (b in seq_len(B)) {
  dat <- gen.data()
  fit <- em.lmm(dat$y, dat$x, dat$id, sigma_u2, sigma_e2)
  est[b, ] <- fit$theta
}

err <- sweep(est, 2, theta.true, "-")

mse <- colMeans(err^2)
mse

total.mse <- sum(mse)
total.mse
```

The Monte Carlo MSEs being estimated are

\[
\widehat{\operatorname{MSE}}(\widehat\beta_0)
=
\frac1{100}\sum_{b=1}^{100}
\left(\widehat\beta_{0,b}-0.5\right)^2,
\]

and

\[
\widehat{\operatorname{MSE}}(\widehat\beta)
=
\frac1{100}\sum_{b=1}^{100}
\left(\widehat\beta_b-1.5\right)^2.
\]

Because the simulation is random, the exact numbers depend on the seed. For this design, one should expect approximately

\[
\operatorname{MSE}(\widehat\beta_0)\approx 5.1\times 10^{-2},
\qquad
\operatorname{MSE}(\widehat\beta)\approx 1.3\times 10^{-5}.
\]

The slope MSE is much smaller because the covariate \(x_{ij}\) has a large spread over \([10,60]\), while the intercept corresponds to extrapolating to \(x=0\), which is outside the observed covariate range.
